title: Potiphar's house (Genesis 39)
hook: Joseph rises, is falsely accused, and lands in prison

segments.voice: Yesterday, Judah and Tamar: a seal, a cord, a staff, and a man who finally said she is more righteous than I. Your line was she was right. Now back to Joseph, a slave in Egypt. Day sixty-eight.

Not long ago Joseph was the favorite son with the fancy coat. Since then he's been thrown in a pit by his own brothers, sold to strangers, carried down to Egypt, and sold again, far from everyone he knows. An Egyptian official named Potiphar, captain of Pharaoh's guard, buys him. Joseph has every reason to shut down. To do the minimum. To be bitter for the rest of his life. Today: what Joseph does instead, and what it costs him.
screen: `FAVORITE SON TO SLAVE.` → `SOLD TO POTIPHAR.` → `EVERY REASON TO SHUT DOWN.`

segments.voice: The chapter opens with a line that becomes its drumbeat: "And the LORD was with Joseph, and he was a prosperous man." Joseph works, and everything he touches goes well. Potiphar notices, and soon puts him in charge of the whole house. Then trouble. Potiphar's wife wants Joseph, and asks him, day after day. He refuses, and his answer is about loyalty and about God: his master trusted him with everything, "how then can I do this great wickedness, and sin against God?" One day, when the house is empty, she grabs his garment. He runs, and leaves it in her hand. And she uses it. She tells the household, and then her husband, that the Hebrew slave attacked her, and holds up the garment as proof. Notice something. This is the second time a piece of Joseph's clothing is used to tell a lie about him. First the coat, dipped in blood. Now this. So Joseph, who did the right thing, lands in prison. And here's the part that makes the chapter. The same line comes back: the LORD was with Joseph. In prison. The keeper of the prison notices him, and soon Joseph is running the place, looking after the other prisoners. Nothing in the story says the pit or the prison was good. What it says is that Joseph kept being Joseph wherever they put him. Honest in the good house. Useful in the bad one.
screen: `THE LORD WAS WITH JOSEPH.` · `HOW CAN I DO THIS GREAT WICKEDNESS?` · `A GARMENT USED TO LIE, AGAIN.` · `IN PRISON, STILL JOSEPH.` · then, large: `GOOD IN THE PIT TOO.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: keep doing good in a bad place. Settle, and breathe. Think of a place in your life that isn't good right now. A job you'd leave if you could. A tense home. A hospital room. A situation that isn't fair. Then think of one small good thing you could still do there. Help one person. Do one task well. Be honest when it's easier not to be. You don't have to pretend the place is fine. The bell holds the time.
Potiphar's house. Where Joseph rose from slave to steward, refused his master's wife, was falsely accused, and was sent to prison.
Your line: good in the pit too. Today, in the hardest room you walk into, do one good thing anyway. Day sixty-eight.

howItsDone: Jewish tradition calls Joseph Yosef ha-Tzaddik, Joseph the righteous, and rabbinic teaching ties the title to how he acted in Potiphar's house.

fork.setup: you're Joseph, a slave now running your master's whole house. your master's wife keeps pressing you, day after day. what do you do?
fork.reveal: he refuses: "how then can I do this great wickedness, and sin against God?" when she grabs his garment he runs, and she uses it to accuse him.

original.note: Hebrew: a garment. the word for what she grabbed and held up as proof (39:12).

trapdoor: what you thought: a story about resisting temptation.
what it means: a story about staying yourself in a bad place. the LORD was with Joseph in the good house and in prison.
what a scholar hears: 'the LORD was with Joseph' frames the chapter (39:2–3, 21, 23). clothing runs through the whole Joseph story: coat, garment, and later Egyptian robes.
